chunks: "I think of it as a pipeline that starts with raw Bayer data and works toward a display-ready picture, in an order that's dictated by the math.
First the raw-domain cleanup, while the data is still linear: subtract the black level, correct the dead and hot pixels, and fix the lens shading, since corners are darker.
Optionally a first noise reduction pass, because noise is easiest to model here.
Next demosaicing: each pixel only has one of red, green or blue, so we interpolate the other two from neighbors, using edge-aware methods to avoid zipper artifacts.
Then color: white balance applies per-channel gains so gray looks gray under the scene's light, and a 3 by 3 color correction matrix maps the sensor's RGB to a standard color space like sRGB.
Only then do we go non-linear: gamma and tone mapping compress the dynamic range into the display range, so shadows and highlights both look right.
After that comes the polish: denoise chroma, sharpen luma, maybe local contrast, then convert to YCbCr, subsample the chroma and compress to JPEG or HEIC.
Running alongside is the statistics engine feeding auto exposure, autofocus and white balance, which close the loop back to the sensor.
In hardware it's a streaming pipeline with a few line buffers rather than a full frame store."
